bates2019mech.title: Bates & Others v Post Office Ltd (No. 6) "Horizon Issues", [2019] EWHC 3408 (QB) — judgment of Fraser J, para 446 (how the Dalmellington bug worked)
bates2019mech.author: The Hon. Mr Justice Fraser
bates2019mech.quote: One related to what is called Forced Log Out, when the Post Log On script was not correctly closed down and was left on the stack of incomplete processes. The other related to the way the Pouch Delivery script operated; because the Post Log On script had not correctly closed down meaning the stack was not empty, the Pouch Delivery script thought it had not finished and attempted to repeat the last part of the script. This had the effect of recording the remittance transactions and printing of receipts. This would lead to duplicate pouch IDs.
supports: the log-on script was left on the stack of incomplete processes
the Pouch Delivery script repeated its last part
each repeat wrote a remittance and printed a receipt
duplicate pouch IDs

bates2019dal.title: Bates & Others v Post Office Ltd (No. 6) "Horizon Issues", [2019] EWHC 3408 (QB) — para 447 (what happened at Dalmellington)
bates2019dal.author: The Hon. Mr Justice Fraser
bates2019dal.quote: What happened at Dalmellington was the SPM scanned £8,000 from her core branch into her outreach branch. She was lucky in this sense, in my judgment, in that she "controlled" both ends of the transaction. The transfer replicated four times. She had Horizon receipts in her outreach branch of £32,000 (4 times £8,000) and therefore a discrepancy of £24,000, as she had only transferred £8,000 in cash out of her core branch into it.
supports: £8,000 scanned once
the transfer replicated four times
receipts of £32,000
a discrepancy of £24,000
the subpostmaster was a woman who controlled both ends

bates2019look.title: Bates & Others v Post Office Ltd (No. 6) "Horizon Issues", [2019] EWHC 3408 (QB) — para 450 (Mr Godeseth's evidence on how the bug presented)
bates2019look.author: The Hon. Mr Justice Fraser
bates2019look.quote: Mr Godeseth said that "Unfortunately this particular error is not subject to receipts and payments problems because it could be -- it could be the user doing something twice, it's -- the bug had the effect of making it look as though a user was simply doing something multiple times."
supports: Fujitsu's Chief Architect told the court the bug looked exactly like a user repeating an action
the duplicates were indistinguishable from legitimate repeats
the error was "not subject to receipts and payments problems" — Horizon's own internal mismatch check did not fire on it

bates2019callendar.title: Bates & Others v Post Office Ltd (No. 6) "Horizon Issues", [2019] EWHC 3408 (QB) — paras 402 and 404 (the Riposte lock problem and Fujitsu's KEL JSimpkins338Q; the Callendar Square / Falkirk branch, from the Area Intervention Manager Visit Log)
bates2019callendar.author: The Hon. Mr Justice Fraser
bates2019callendar.quote: [402] One of the KELs to which he was taken, with the reference JSimpkins338Q, related to problems with Riposte and what was sometimes called the Riposte lock or unlock problem. This was when an unexpected error occurred in Riposte while attempting to insert a message. […] Under "solution" in the KEL the following entry appears: "[…] Warn the PM that if transactions appear to be missing, they should not be re-entered - they will become visible after the counter has been rebooted." [404] The Callendar Square issue or consequences (now admitted by the Post Office to be a bug) were discovered in 2005 at the Callendar Square branch (hence the name). It is also sometimes called the Falkirk bug […] "This was picked up when a member of staff noticed that a transaction, which had been taken by another member of staff, had not been entered onto the system, so therefore she put the transaction through. […] Following on from that, it was picked up that other giro business deposits that had been entered had not come up on the system, so they were re-keyed. There was also a problem with transfers from one stock to another, in that they had doubled up. […] The result was that the office balanced £6,414.46 short."
supports: the bug was discovered in 2005 at the Callendar Square branch, also called the Falkirk bug
the Riposte lock/unlock problem was an unexpected error inserting a message
staff re-keyed transactions that appeared not to have gone through
transfers doubled up
the branch balanced £6,414.46 short
Fujitsu's own support note told staff to warn postmasters not to re-enter apparently missing transactions, because they reappear after the counter is rebooted

bates2019risk.title: Bates & Others v Post Office Ltd (No. 6) "Horizon Issues", [2019] EWHC 3408 (QB) — para 970 (the finding on Horizon Issue 1)
bates2019risk.author: The Hon. Mr Justice Fraser
bates2019risk.quote: I accept the claimants' submissions that, in terms of likelihood, there was a significant and material risk on occasion of branch accounts being affected in the way alleged by the claimants by bugs, errors and defects.

bates2019misra.title: Bates & Others v Post Office Ltd (No. 6) "Horizon Issues", [2019] EWHC 3408 (QB) — para 77 (the criminal trial of Mrs Seema Misra)
bates2019misra.author: The Hon. Mr Justice Fraser
bates2019misra.quote: Mr McLachlan had been called as an expert witness in the criminal trial of Mrs Seema Misra, a SPM at West Byfleet in Surrey who was charged both with theft from her branch, and also false accounting. […] The sums in question were approximately £74,000. Mrs Misra pleaded not guilty, and her defence was that the Horizon system was to blame. She was convicted by a jury after a trial in late 2010 at Guildford Crown Court, and was sentenced to a term of imprisonment of 15 months. She was pregnant at the time of her conviction and imprisonment. Expert evidence was called by the Post Office at her trial from Mr Gareth Jenkins from Fujitsu.
supports: Seema Misra, subpostmistress at West Byfleet, Surrey
approximately £74,000
convicted by a jury in late 2010 at Guildford Crown Court
15 months' imprisonment
pregnant at conviction
Fujitsu's Gareth Jenkins gave expert evidence for the prosecution

inquiry2025acts.title: Post Office Horizon IT Inquiry Report: Volume 1 (HC 1119, ordered to be printed 8 July 2025) — paras 4.1, 4.8 and 4.236 (the statutory exoneration Acts, their extent, and the HCRS)
inquiry2025acts.author: Sir Wyn Williams
inquiry2025acts.quote: [4.1] a scheme to provide financial redress for those whose convictions have been quashed under the provisions of the Post Office (Horizon System) Offences Act 2024 and the Post Office (Horizon System Offences (Scotland)) Act 2024, known as the Horizon Conviction Redress Scheme (“HCRS”) [4.8] On 24 May 2024, the Post Office (Horizon System) Offences Act 2024 came into force in England, Wales and Northern Ireland. Shortly thereafter, the Post Office (Horizon System (Scotland)) Offences Act 2024 became the law in Scotland. The effect of this legislation is that the convictions of hundreds of persons have been quashed. On 30 July 2024, HCRS was launched … [4.236] Those whose convictions have been quashed by the Post Office (Horizon System) Offences Act 2024 in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, and by the Post Office (Horizon System) Offences (Scotland) Act 2024 in Scotland, are eligible to claim financial redress.
supports: convictions quashed by statute in 2024
Post Office (Horizon System) Offences Act 2024 extends to England, Wales and Northern Ireland
Post Office (Horizon System) Offences (Scotland) Act 2024 covers Scotland
both routed claimants into the Horizon Conviction Redress Scheme, launched 30 July 2024

inquiry2025hss.title: Post Office Horizon IT Inquiry Report: Volume 1 (HC 1119, ordered to be printed 8 July 2025) — para 4.133 (Horizon Shortfall Scheme payouts)
inquiry2025hss.author: Sir Wyn Williams
inquiry2025hss.quote: As of 30 April 2025, there have been a total of 9,437 eligible claims submitted in HSS. According to the information published on GOV.UK, 6,644 offers have been made, and 5,812 offers have been accepted (of which 5,725 have been paid). A total of £507m (made up of full and final awards and interim payments) had been paid out to claimants.
supports: £507m paid out under the Horizon Shortfall Scheme as at 30 April 2025
9,437 eligible claims

unverified: The allocation brief's figure of "three £8,000 transfers instead of one" at Dalmellington. The judgment at para 447 says the transfer replicated four times, giving receipts of £32,000 and a discrepancy of £24,000; the brief's number is not used.

The allocation brief's figures of "over 900 subpostmasters prosecuted", "236 imprisoned" and "at least four suicides". Sir Wyn Williams puts prosecutions and convictions at approximately 1,000 (Volume 1, para 3.24) and records six former postmasters named by the Post Office as having taken their own lives (para 3.8); no figure for imprisonments was found in the sources opened, so none is claimed.

The often-quoted aggregate compensation figure of "over £1bn". Volume 1 gives per-scheme totals at differing dates (£507m HSS, £229m, £160m, £68m) and no single aggregate, so only the HSS figure is used and only on a card.

The exact date in 2015 of the Dalmellington incident itself. The judgment dates the discovery and the Fujitsu investigation to 2015 and the bug's effects to 2010-2015, but gives no day or month for the branch event.
That Dalmellington is in East Ayrshire, Scotland. True as a matter of geography but not stated in the judgment, so no county or country appears in the prose.

The number of times Fujitsu actually did inject or amend branch transaction data. Mr Godeseth's evidence was that he could not work out the number of times this may have happened (para 399), and the court made no finding on frequency.

Whether the Callendar Square re-keying at the Falkirk branch on 14.09.05 was itself caused by the Riposte lock bug rather than by staff error. The Area Intervention Manager's log records the sequence; the judgment treats Callendar Square as an admitted bug but does not attribute every re-keyed line to it, so the prose describes the pattern, not a causal finding for that specific branch.

What kind of premises the Dalmellington outreach branch was. Para 445 describes outreach branches generically as "a mobile post office van, or village hall somewhere else"; the judgment never says which Dalmellington's was, so the prose says only "outreach branch".

Whether Fujitsu's KEL warning that apparently missing transactions "should not be re-entered" pre-dated the Callendar Square re-keying on 14.09.05. Para 402 says the KEL (JSimpkins338Q) ran from 2002 with events in 2003, 2004 and 2005, but does not date the "solution" entry that carries the warning, so no claim is made that Fujitsu had published it before the branch re-keyed.

The date on which subpostmasters' transaction and event log retention changed from 42 days to 60. Para 999 gives both figures and no changeover date; the prose uses the later, more generous 60-day figure, which is the one in force by the 2015 Dalmellington incident on any reading.

The exact statutory short title of the Scottish Act. Volume 1 renders it three different ways — "Post Office (Horizon System Offences (Scotland)) Act 2024" (para 4.1), "Post Office (Horizon System (Scotland)) Offences Act 2024" (para 4.8) and "Post Office (Horizon System) Offences (Scotland) Act 2024" (para 4.236). legislation.gov.uk returned HTTP 202 with no body to every request, so the card uses the para 4.236 rendering, which is the only one that parses and which matches the UK Act's naming.

The closing year of the Dalmellington bug's effects. The Technical Appendix (Bug 4) says "The years of its effect were 2010 to 2015"; para 450 says "the effects of this bug were experienced for the period from 2010 until 2016" and para 449 records a fix applied in January 2016. The card quotes the Technical Appendix and claims no end date beyond it.

Sources dropped from this ledger when the story was re-aimed onto the books-versus-cash mismatch: the 42/60-day limit on subpostmasters' transaction logs (para 999), Fujitsu's ability to inject branch transaction data (paras 1003-1004), and Sir Wyn Williams' figure of approximately 1,000 persons prosecuted and convicted (Volume 1, para 3.24). All three were opened and verified; none is claimed in the current prose or on a card. The fourth dropped entry, para 402's KEL warning that apparently missing transactions "should not be re-entered", is still claimed on card p2c02-c3, so it was folded into the bates2019callendar quote rather than deleted.

How many occurrences of the Dalmellington bug there were. The prose reports what Fujitsu found when it investigated — 112 occurrences across 88 branches in the previous 5 years (para 448) — while the Technical Appendix gives the court's own count as "over 110 … (the actual number is probably 116, but at least 114)" with the same 88 branches, which is the figure card p2c02-c2 carries. Both numbers are in the judgment; neither is reconciled there, so each is attributed to the paragraph it comes from.

The allocation brief's claim that "every phantom entry had a counterpart", i.e. that each duplicate remittance was a balanced double entry. Horizon did run a double-entry constraint as one of its checks (paras 846 and 880 name "Double entry accounting – DEA"), and a faithful repeat of a legitimate remittance would satisfy it, but the judgment never says this of the Dalmellington duplicates — and the only paragraph that discusses the DEA check failing to catch a bug (para 880, on the Receipts/Payments Mismatch bug) says it failed because that operation was "apparently not a double-entry operation on the BRDB", the opposite case. The prose therefore claims only what Mr Godeseth testified at para 450: the entries looked like a user repeating an action, and the error was "not subject to receipts and payments problems".
